facts: Woodcock migrate alone, at night. Each bird lifts off around dusk, flies a few hours through the dark, and drops into thick cover before dawn — there are no flocks, no V formations, no daytime movements.

They fly absurdly low for a migrant: roughly 50 to 300 meters up, skimming the treetops where songbirds pass thousands of feet overhead. The woodcock also holds the record for the slowest flight speed ever measured in a bird, about 5 mph during its courtship display.

Migration is a chain of habitat, not a single flight: hops of 20 to 150 miles separated by multi-day stopovers in young forest, aspen cuts, alder runs, and river-bottom thickets. Lose the stopover cover and the chain breaks.

GPS-tagged birds show real stopover fidelity — some return to the same few acres of covert or the same wintering field in consecutive years, navigating back to a patch of mud they last probed twelve months earlier.

The Eastern Woodcock Migration Research Cooperative, coordinated by the University of Maine since 2017, has fitted 737 woodcock with 4.5-gram rump-mounted GPS-Argos transmitters across 15 states and 3 Canadian provinces, producing the first full-annual-cycle picture of the species' movements.

The bird collects nicknames the way it collects earthworms: timberdoodle, bogsucker, night partridge, Labrador twister. Its eyes sit high and far back on its skull so it can watch the sky for hawks while its bill is buried in the mud — an arrangement so extreme its brain is effectively upside-down.

The flyways sort themselves in fall: Atlantic birds funnel down the coastal lowlands — stacking up at bay crossings like Cape May to wait for a north wind — and winter in the Carolinas and Georgia, while Great Lakes birds ride the Mississippi's river bottoms south to the piney woods of Louisiana and east Texas, the species' wintering stronghold.
